title: Roman Is Off the Pad
hook: NASA's Roman Space Telescope is on its way to L2, a million miles out. Its trick is speed: it surveys the sky roughly a thousand times faster than Hubble, at about 1.4 terabytes a day.
key_points: Roman has launched on a million-mile cruise to the Sun-Earth L2 point.
Survey speed is roughly 1,000 times Hubble's, at comparable sharpness.
It will stream about 1.4 terabytes of data per day back to Earth.
Core science: dark matter, dark energy, and finding distant exoplanets.
Wide, fast surveys are how you test dark energy — you need millions of galaxies, not deep stares.
At that survey rate, the mission is expected to turn up phenomena nobody planned for.
content_html: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has launched, beginning a million-mile trip to the L2 point beyond Earth's night side. It carries a Hubble-class mirror, but its design goal is not depth — it is coverage. Roman can survey huge swathes of sky roughly a thousand times faster than Hubble, firehosing about 1.4 terabytes of data back to Earth each day.
extra_html: That speed is what the mission's headline science needs. Dark energy and dark matter are measured statistically: you map how millions of galaxies are distributed and weakly lensed, and read the expansion history off the pattern. A telescope that stares deeply at one small patch cannot do that; one that maps continent-sized areas of sky can. The same survey data will also catch exoplanets by microlensing, including worlds on wide orbits that other techniques miss. As ScienceDaily notes, an instrument that scans this much sky this fast is also the kind that turns up things nobody was looking for.

related.title: NASA's Roman Telescope Is Cleared to Launch
related.hook: Hubble sees deep; Roman is built to see wide. NASA has cleared its next flagship observatory for a late-August launch to map cosmic expansion across huge swathes of sky.

related.title: Dark Matter & Dark Energy
related.hook: Everything we can see — stars, planets, people — is only about 5% of the universe. The other 95% is two mysteries we've never directly detected.

related.title: Is Dark Energy Changing Over Time?
related.hook: For decades dark energy looked like a constant. New galaxy-survey data hints it may evolve — and that would shift even our measured value of the cosmic expansion rate.

related.title: The Expanding Universe
related.hook: Distant galaxies are rushing away from us, and the farther one is, the faster it flees — not because they're moving through space, but because space itself is stretching.

flashcards.prompt: What is Roman's main advantage over Hubble?

choices.text: It surveys the sky roughly a thousand times faster at similar sharpness
It sees much fainter objects in a single long exposure
It observes gamma rays instead of infrared light

flashcards.explanation_html: Roman trades nothing in resolution but covers enormously more sky per hour — about 1,000x Hubble's survey speed — which is what dark energy studies need.

flashcards.prompt: Why does testing dark energy require a wide survey rather than a deep one?
flashcards.back_html: You need statistics on millions of galaxies to measure how the expansion rate changed over cosmic time; a few very deep stares at small patches cannot deliver that.

flashcards.prompt: Where is Roman headed, and roughly how far is that?
flashcards.back_html: The Sun-Earth L2 point, about a million miles from Earth — the same gravitational parking spot used by JWST.
